nodes.ask: Acute weakness in the ED. First moves?
options: Airway, swallow, breathing and a fingerstick glucose; then the bloods
Pulse oximetry and an arterial blood gas to judge how well the patient breathes
Non-contrast CT of the head, with the glucose added to the main lab panel
A urine drug screen first, as intoxication can mimic the weakness
nodes.chainStep: Check airway, cough and swallow; fingerstick glucose; if the weakness is generalized or bulbar, bedside FVC with maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures, repeated (end-tidal CO2 in an infant); a sudden focal deficit goes straight to the stroke pathway for immediate imaging; electrolytes with magnesium and phosphate, blood count, kidney and liver tests
nodes.why: Breathing is measured, not judged by eye: not every patient heading for respiratory failure is breathless, and the oximeter and the blood gas can stay normal until late, because hypoxia and hypercapnia come late in neuromuscular failure. A weak face or bulbar muscles can block the upper airway before the diaphragm fails. Hypoglycemia is excluded in anyone with sudden neurological symptoms, and every suspected GBS gets a blood count, glucose, electrolytes, kidney and liver tests, with magnesium and phosphate because both can cause acute weakness. A sudden focal deficit is a suspected stroke, diagnosed rapidly in the stroke pathway. Intoxication is one of the things weakness gets mistaken for, but the breathing and the glucose come first.

orders.item: Bedside spirometry, generalized or bulbar weakness
orders.dose: Serial vital capacity, maximal inspiratory and maximal expiratory pressure; at risk of respiratory failure if FVC under 20 mL/kg, MIP under 30 cm H2O or MEP under 40 cm H2O (the 20/30/40 rule)

orders.item: Face too weak to seal the mouthpiece
orders.dose: Use a mask device; without spirometry, the single breath count or sniff nasal inspiratory pressure
Continuous end-tidal CO2 is the most effective bedside measure of respiratory depression
Not reliable early markers: hypoxia and hypercapnia can come late in neuromuscular respiratory failure
Glucose, electrolytes with magnesium and phosphate, blood count, kidney and liver tests, thyroid function

nodes.note: Not in this version: trauma, poisoning and toxidromes including organophosphates (the toxicology pathway, pw_tox), weakness in critical illness, chronic or slowly progressive weakness, and children beyond infant botulism.

sources.where: Diagnosis of botulism; Key points for clinicians; Respiratory monitoring

nodes.label: Breathing, bulbar function, glucose, potassium and the first exam

outcomes.if: Breathing at risk; FVC under 20 mL/kg, MIP under 30 or MEP under 40 cm H2O, or pooled secretions
Drowsy, shocked or arrhythmic; reduced consciousness, low pressure or an unstable rhythm
Glucose low; under 72 mg/dL (4 mmol/L) on the fingerstick

orders.dose: Blood glucose under 72 mg/dL (4.0 mmol/L), treated without delay

sources.where: Treatment of hypoglycaemia algorithms; Management of hypoglycaemia

outcomes.if: Potassium abnormal; low or high, with flaccid weakness
Sudden focal weakness; one side of the face, arm or leg
Cord signs with a red flag; a level with cancer, fever or drug use, or saddle loss with no level

orders.dose: Dexamethasone 16 mg orally (or the parenteral equivalent) as soon as possible; MRI as soon as possible and always within 24 hours
Emergency MRI as soon as possible and certainly within 4 hours of the request

outcomes.if: Sensory level, no red flag; no cancer, fever or drug use, with or without bladder change
No breathing cutoff crossed; glucose and potassium normal, no pooled secretions, no sudden focal deficit, no cord or saddle signs

nodes.summary: Low glucose with weakness: correct it now; the altered mental status pathway (pw_ams) has the doses. Weakness that persists once the glucose is normal starts this pathway again, and a sudden focal deficit goes to the stroke pathway (pw_stroke).

Weakness with an abnormal potassium. Low-potassium paralysis from a shift (periodic paralysis, including thyrotoxic): oral potassium chloride first; IV only for arrhythmia, a failed swallow or respiratory weakness, as 40 mEq/L in 5% mannitol at no more than 20 mEq/h, at most 200 mEq in 24 hours, on continuous ECG, with potassium followed for 24 hours, because total body potassium is not depleted and aggressive repletion risks rebound hyperkalemia; ECG and thyroid tests at a first attack. In thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, treatment of the hyperthyroidism is the mainstay. Other potassium emergencies: pw_electrolytes.
Resuscitate first; a drowsy patient goes to pw_ams; altered consciousness argues against GBS.
Sudden focal weakness: the stroke pathway (pw_stroke) takes it from here, with the glucose checked, the time last known well fixed, and immediate imaging.

Cord or cauda equina signs with a red flag: the back pain pathway (pw_back_pain) takes it from here: dexamethasone 16 mg now and an MRI within 24 hours for known cancer, an emergency MRI within 4 hours of the request for suspected cauda equina syndrome, and its infection route for fever or injection drug use.

nodes.ask: Breathing at risk: FVC under 20 mL/kg, weak MIP or pooled secretions. Next?
options: Admit to the ICU and support the breathing before the blood gas fails
High-flow oxygen on a general ward, with hourly pulse oximetry checks
IVIG now, since immunotherapy is what reverses the weakness
Noninvasive ventilation on a general medical ward, with nursing checks
nodes.chainStep: Admit to the ICU; support ventilation now (in GBS intubate, no succinylcholine; in myasthenic crisis noninvasive ventilation first if parameters allow); aspiration precautions; serial FVC, MIP and MEP
nodes.why: Evolving respiratory distress with imminent respiratory insufficiency, severe swallowing trouble or a weak cough are reasons for intensive care, and in GBS up to 22% need ventilation within the first week. The oximeter and the gas are late markers, so waiting for them, or treating with oxygen on a ward, waits too long. IVIG is slow to act and is not the treatment for botulism, so it does not come before the airway. In GBS noninvasive ventilation is not recommended and succinylcholine is avoided because it can cause hyperkalemia; in myasthenic crisis noninvasive ventilation can come first if parameters allow, escalating quickly to intubation in intensive care; in botulism paralytics are avoided or used only after careful thought.

orders.dose: Indicated with impending respiratory failure: the 20/30/40 rule, a weak cough, accessory muscle use, PaCO2 over 48 mm Hg or PaO2 under 56 mm Hg; noninvasive ventilation not recommended
Avoid during intubation; it can precipitate hyperkalemia
Noninvasive ventilation first if parameters allow; intubate in intensive care if they fail to improve or the patient tires
Resistant to succinylcholine and highly sensitive to nondepolarizing agents such as rocuronium; dose carefully
Avoid, or use only after careful consideration with appropriate monitoring
Induction agents and doses are not in the sources read

nodes.note: Patients paralyzed by GBS or botulism are usually fully conscious: explain each procedure.

nodes.label: Glucose, potassium and cord signs, breathing supported

outcomes.if: Glucose low; hypoglycemia on the fingerstick
Potassium abnormal; low or high, with flaccid weakness
Cord signs with a red flag; a level with cancer, fever or drug use, or saddle loss, breathing supported

orders.dose: Dexamethasone 16 mg orally (or the parenteral equivalent) as soon as possible; MRI as soon as possible and always within 24 hours
Emergency MRI as soon as possible and certainly within 4 hours of the request

outcomes.if: Sensory level, no red flag; no cancer, fever or drug use, breathing supported
Glucose, potassium and cord exam normal; no sensory level

nodes.ask: Sensory level, no cancer, fever or drug use. Imaging?
options: Emergency MRI of the whole spine, without and with gadolinium
Non-contrast CT of the head to rule out a stroke as the cause
Lumbar puncture for CSF cells and protein before the imaging
Plain thoracic spine x-rays to look for a collapsed vertebra
nodes.chainStep: Emergency MRI of the whole spine without and with gadolinium; brain MRI with and without gadolinium if myelitis is found
nodes.why: A sharp sensory level points to the spinal cord and casts doubt on GBS. A compressive lesion has to be excluded first, and that is done by MRI, not by a head CT, a lumbar puncture or plain films: the whole spine with and without gadolinium separates compressive from non-compressive lesions.

sources.where: Table: features that argue against GBS

outcomes.if: Cord compression; a disc, mass or collection presses on the cord
Myelitis, no compression; T2 signal within the cord
No cord lesion; no compression and no signal change

nodes.summary: Cord compression on MRI: an emergency for the spinal surgeons. Metastatic compression (dexamethasone 16 mg as soon as possible) and epidural abscess follow pw_back_pain; a disc or other benign compression goes straight to the spinal team.

nodes.ask: Cord signal on MRI, no compression. Next?
options: High-dose IV steroids now, with the LP and antibody tests sent alongside
Emergency decompressive laminectomy at the level of the cord signal change
Dexamethasone 16 mg and radiotherapy to the cord lesion within 24 hours
Plasma exchange as the first treatment, before a glucocorticoid
nodes.chainStep: High-dose IV methylprednisolone or dexamethasone now, for 3 to 5 days; LP (cells, protein, glucose, VDRL, oligoclonal bands, IgG index, cytology); brain MRI with and without gadolinium; serum AQP4 and MOG antibodies, B12, methylmalonic acid, ANA, Ro, La, syphilis, HIV, TSH; plasma exchange if no response
nodes.why: Once compression is excluded, high-dose IV glucocorticoids are the first-line treatment and start as soon as possible, without waiting for the test results. Plasma exchange is for disease that fails to respond to steroids. There is nothing to decompress, and dexamethasone with radiotherapy treats metastatic compression, which the MRI has excluded.

orders.dose: High dose, as soon as possible, methylprednisolone or dexamethasone for 3 to 5 days
The mg dose is not stated in the source read
If the myelitis fails to respond to glucocorticoids

Brain MRI with and without gadolinium; LP with cells, protein, glucose, VDRL, oligoclonal bands, IgG index and cytology; serum AQP4 and MOG antibodies, B12, methylmalonic acid, ANA, Ro, La, syphilis, HIV, TSH
Urinary retention may be the first sign of myelitis; check for it

nodes.summary: Transverse myelitis: compression excluded on MRI, high-dose IV glucocorticoids without waiting for results, plasma exchange if they fail, and a search for multiple sclerosis, NMOSD (AQP4 antibodies), MOG antibody disease, infection and systemic autoimmune disease. About a third recover with little or no deficit, a third keep a moderate permanent disability and a third are permanently disabled.

Sensory level with a normal spine MRI: neither compression nor myelitis is shown, so other causes come back into play. A sharp sensory level argues against GBS, but GBS can show enhancing nerve roots on gadolinium MRI and a raised CSF protein. Not covered further in this version.

nodes.ask: Breathing measures safe or supported; glucose and potassium normal. Next?
options: History of infection, food, wounds and drugs; pupils, reflexes, skin search
Send antiganglioside antibodies, and let that result decide the treatment
Nerve conduction studies first, ahead of a detailed bedside examination
MRI of the brain and whole spine with gadolinium as the opening investigation
nodes.chainStep: History: onset and direction of spread, infection in the last 6 weeks, home-canned food, injection drug use and wounds, medicines, outdoor exposure; exam: pupils, eye movements, bulbar muscles, fatigability, reflexes, sensation, and a full skin search for a tick
nodes.why: The bedside pattern sorts the causes. GBS is rapidly progressive bilateral weakness, usually rising from the legs, with reduced or absent reflexes, and two thirds report an infection in the 6 weeks before. Botulism is symmetric cranial nerve palsies, then descending weakness, in an alert, afebrile patient, and unreactive pupils are expected but not always seen; home-canned food and injection drug use are the classic exposures. In myasthenia the weakness fluctuates and the pupils, reflexes and sensation are normal. Tick paralysis mimics GBS, so the scalp, axillae, between the digits and the perineum are searched. Antiganglioside antibodies are of limited value and treatment does not wait for them; nerve conduction can be normal in the first week; and MRI is not routine in GBS.

orders.dose: Scalp (most often behind the ears), axillae, between the digits and the perineum; there may be more than one tick

sources.where: History and physical; Pearls and other issues

orders.dose: Ask about home-canned food and injection drug use; their absence does not rule botulism out

sources.where: Diagnosis of botulism; Exposure risk factors

outcomes.if: Ascending, reflexes reduced or absent, no tick; legs first, mild sensory change, normal pupils
Ascending, reflexes absent, tick attached; found on the skin search
Known myasthenia, weaker; fatigable ptosis or bulbar weakness, reflexes present
Myasthenia, new and untreated; fatigable ptosis, diplopia or bulbar weakness, reflexes present
Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia; little limb weakness
Descending, afebrile and alert; cranial nerve palsies first, sensation normal
Floppy infant under 1 year; constipation, weak suck and cry
Inconsistent weakness; positive Hoover sign, normal reflexes and tone
None of these patterns; for example tender proximal muscles, dark urine

nodes.summary: Miller Fisher syndrome, the GBS variant of ophthalmoplegia, areflexia and ataxia: usually mild, and most recover completely without treatment within 6 months, so treatment is generally not recommended; monitor closely, because a subgroup goes on to limb weakness, bulbar or facial palsy, or respiratory failure. Anti-GQ1b antibodies are found in up to 90%.
Not covered in this version: inflammatory myositis, rhabdomyolysis, toxic myopathy (statins, colchicine), and low phosphate or high magnesium, all on the GBS differential.

nodes.ask: Ascending weakness, reflexes reduced or absent, no tick found. Next test?
options: Lumbar puncture for CSF protein and cells; nerve conduction studies
Stool culture for Campylobacter to confirm the infection that triggered it
Contrast MRI of the brain as the test that confirms the diagnosis
Serum creatine kinase and a muscle biopsy from the weakest muscle
nodes.chainStep: Lumbar puncture: CSF protein and cell count (before IVIG if possible); nerve conduction studies, repeated in 2 to 3 weeks if normal early
nodes.why: CSF examination belongs in the initial evaluation, mainly to rule out other causes; the classic finding is a raised protein with a normal cell count. Nerve conduction studies are not required but are recommended wherever possible, and can be normal in the first week. Testing for the preceding infection does not usually help the diagnosis, MRI is not part of the routine workup, and GBS is a disease of the peripheral nerves and nerve roots, not muscle.

orders.dose: Protein and cell count; protein is normal in 30 to 50% in the first week, so a normal protein does not rule GBS out
IVIG can raise CSF protein and white cells, complicating interpretation
Wherever possible; may be normal within 1 week of onset
Limited value; do not wait for the result before treating

outcomes.if: Protein raised, cells normal; albuminocytologic dissociation
Protein and cells normal; within 2 weeks of onset
Cells 10 to 50 per microliter; mild pleocytosis

orders.dose: Compatible with GBS but should prompt alternative diagnoses such as infectious polyradiculitis

outcomes.if: Cells over 50 per microliter; marked pleocytosis

nodes.summary: Marked CSF pleocytosis, over 50 cells per microliter, points away from GBS: look for leptomeningeal malignancy or an infection or inflammation of the cord or nerve roots (Lyme disease, CMV, HIV among them). Not covered further in this version.

outcomes.if: Cannot walk 10 m unaided; within 2 weeks of the onset of weakness
Cannot walk 10 m, 2 to 4 weeks from onset; plasma exchange window
Walks 10 m unaided; no rapid progression, bulbar, autonomic or breathing trouble
Walks 10 m but worsening fast; or autonomic, bulbar or breathing trouble

nodes.summary: Plasma exchange has trial evidence when started within 4 weeks; IVIG trials covered the first 2 weeks, and beyond these windows evidence is lacking.
Evidence is limited, but immunotherapy should be considered.

Mild GBS, still walking 10 m unaided: the evidence for immunotherapy is limited, but it should be considered if the weakness progresses rapidly or autonomic, bulbar or respiratory trouble appears; keep measuring the breathing and watching the rhythm and blood pressure.

nodes.ask: GBS, cannot walk 10 m unaided, within 2 weeks of onset. Treatment?
options: IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days, or a course of plasma exchange
High-dose IV methylprednisolone, then a tapering oral steroid
Plasma exchange, followed straight away by a full IVIG course
Supportive care, with immunotherapy kept for ventilated patients
nodes.chainStep: IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days (or plasma exchange 200 to 250 mL/kg over five sessions); serial FVC, MIP and MEP; swallow and cough checks; continuous ECG, heart rate and blood pressure; bowel and bladder; DVT prevention
nodes.why: Immunotherapy starts when the patient cannot walk 10 m unaided: IVIG within 2 weeks of the onset of weakness and plasma exchange within 4 weeks are equally effective, and IVIG is usually chosen because it is easier to give. Eight trials of corticosteroids showed no benefit and oral steroids worsened outcome. Plasma exchange followed by IVIG is no better than either alone. Waiting for a ventilator misses the treatment threshold.

orders.dose: 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days, started within 2 weeks of the onset of weakness
200 to 250 mL plasma per kg over five sessions, started within 4 weeks
Avoid: large fluid shifts can cause hypotension
Not beneficial; oral corticosteroids worsened outcome
IgA deficiency with antibodies against IgA and a history of hypersensitivity
Thrombosis and renal dysfunction (boxed warning); the Gamunex-C label lists PI, ITP and CIDP, not GBS
Vital capacity, MIP and MEP; neck, arm and leg strength; swallow and cough; ECG, heart rate, blood pressure, bowel and bladder
Standard-practice prevention of pressure ulcers, hospital infections and deep vein thrombosis
Not in the sources read

nodes.note: The EAN/PNS 2023 GBS guideline was not readable here; the doses are from the 2019 international ten-step guideline.

nodes.label: Serial breathing, swallow and autonomic checks

outcomes.if: ICU criteria met; FVC under 20 mL/kg, dysautonomia, bulbar palsy or fast decline
No ICU criteria; FVC steady over 20 mL/kg, swallow and rhythm normal

nodes.summary: GBS needing intensive care: IVIG or plasma exchange, ventilation when respiratory failure is imminent (no succinylcholine), and continuous ECG and blood pressure for dysautonomia. The EGRIS estimates the chance of ventilation within a week. About 80% walk independently at 6 months.

GBS stable on the ward: IVIG or plasma exchange, with serial FVC, MIP and MEP, swallow and cough checks, ECG and blood pressure; move to intensive care if respiratory, bulbar or autonomic failure appears. Up to two thirds of GBS deaths come in the recovery phase, from arrhythmias, blood pressure swings or mucus plugs.

nodes.ask: Ascending, areflexic weakness and an engorged tick attached. Next?
options: Remove the whole tick with fine forceps, then search for any others
IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days to stop the ascending paralysis
Doxycycline by mouth, leaving the tick in place for the lab to identify
Watch it for 24 hours first, since weakness can worsen after removal
nodes.chainStep: Remove the tick: fine forceps close to the skin, gentle steady upward and outward traction, no mouthparts left; search for more ticks; supportive care with serial breathing measures
nodes.why: Removing the tick is the treatment: fine forceps close to the skin with gentle, steady upward and outward traction, leaving no mouthparts behind. Patients can carry more than one tick. Plasmapheresis and immune globulin do not help, and antibiotics treat tick-borne infections, which fever or a rash would suggest, not the toxin. Removal is the treatment, done now; Australian Ixodes holocyclus paralysis can worsen after removal, and that is watched in hospital after the tick is out.

orders.dose: Fine forceps close to the skin, gentle steady upward and outward traction, no mouthparts left in the wound
Not helpful in tick paralysis
Supportive care; ventilation in severe cases; Australian Ixodes holocyclus paralysis can worsen for 24 to 48 hours after removal
Rare in tick paralysis; raises suspicion of a tick-borne infection

sources.where: History and physical; Treatment / management; Pearls and other issues

nodes.summary: Tick paralysis: the whole tick removed and the skin searched for more. With North American Dermacentor ticks most recover fully within hours; Australian Ixodes holocyclus paralysis can worsen for 24 to 48 hours after removal, so the breathing is watched as an inpatient. If the weakness does not lift, look for a second tick and reconsider the differential: GBS, botulism, myasthenia and spinal cord lesions.

nodes.ask: Known MG on pyridostigmine, weaker over days. Next?
options: Look for cholinergic signs and a trigger before any more pyridostigmine
Raise the pyridostigmine dose, as weakness in MG means underdosing
Start high-dose prednisone today to treat the myasthenic exacerbation
Start levofloxacin to cover a chest infection as the most likely trigger
nodes.chainStep: Hold further pyridostigmine increases; examine for cholinergic signs (small pupils, salivation, bronchial secretions, sweating, diarrhea, cramps, fasciculations, slow pulse); look for a trigger: infection, a new drug, a recent dose change
nodes.why: Weakness on pyridostigmine can be underdosing or overdosing, and the two crises look alike: more anticholinesterase in a cholinergic crisis can have grave consequences, so the cholinergic signs are looked for first. Infection and drugs (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium) are common triggers; fluoroquinolones have neuromuscular blocking activity and are avoided in MG. Steroids started alone can transiently worsen weakness early in a crisis.

orders.dose: Not until cholinergic crisis is excluded: a failure to improve can mean overdose
Impending or manifest crisis: a monitoring or intensive care unit with neuromuscular experience

nodes.label: Pupils, secretions, drug chart and infection screen

outcomes.if: Cholinergic signs; small pupils, secretions, fasciculations, slow pulse
Trigger found, no cholinergic signs; an infection or a culprit drug

orders.dose: Treat it, avoiding fluoroquinolones (avoid in MG) and aminoglycosides (use with caution in MG)
Stop it where possible: fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, magnesium (prolongs paralysis in MG)

outcomes.if: No trigger, no cholinergic signs; afebrile, no new drug

nodes.ask: Small pupils, secretions, fasciculations and a slow pulse on pyridostigmine. Next?
options: Stop all anticholinesterases, give atropine, and support breathing
Double the pyridostigmine, since this is undertreated myasthenia
IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days for the worsening myasthenia
Neostigmine IV, a faster-acting anticholinesterase than pyridostigmine
nodes.chainStep: Stop all anticholinesterases; atropine IV for the muscarinic effects, repeated until the secretions dry; secure the airway if secretions block it or the respiratory muscles fail; ICU
nodes.why: Cholinergic crisis is overdose: muscarinic signs (small pupils, salivation and bronchial secretions, a slow pulse) with nicotinic cramps, fasciculation and weakness. All anticholinesterases are stopped and atropine is given; atropine does not reverse the nicotinic weakness, so ventilation may be needed. More pyridostigmine or neostigmine adds to the overdose, and IVIG treats a myasthenic crisis, not this.

orders.dose: Stop all of them at once
Adults typically 2 mg, children about 0.03 to 0.05 mg/kg, repeated until the secretions dry; it does not act on nicotinic receptors
orders.note: StatPearls titrates to atropinization (tachycardia, dry flushed skin, mydriasis); the pralidoxime label (pw_tox) titrates to inhibited secretions or atropine toxicity; neither is specific to pyridostigmine excess.

orders.dose: Intubate for secretions that block the airway, GCS under 8, hemodynamic instability or profound respiratory muscle weakness
Masks the signs of overdose and can lead into cholinergic crisis

nodes.summary: Cholinergic crisis from pyridostigmine excess: every anticholinesterase stopped, atropine for the muscarinic effects, and the breathing supported, since atropine does not reverse the nicotinic weakness. Atropine taken routinely for side effects can hide the warning signs.

nodes.ask: Myasthenic crisis or impending crisis, no cholinergic signs. Treatment?
options: IVIG or plasma exchange in intensive care, treating any trigger
IV methylprednisolone as the first treatment, without IVIG or exchange
Urgent thymectomy this admission to remove the antibody source
Start or raise pyridostigmine, and admit to a general medical ward
nodes.chainStep: ICU; IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days (or 1 g/kg daily for 2 days) or plasma exchange; treat the trigger; continuous respiratory and bulbar watch; steroids only alongside IVIG or plasma exchange
nodes.why: Impending and manifest myasthenic crisis are treated in a monitoring or intensive care unit with IVIG or plasma exchange, which are equally effective. Steroids alone can transiently worsen weakness early, so they are added alongside IVIG or plasma exchange, and very high doses are kept for a delayed or poor response. Thymectomy waits until the patient is off the ventilator and stable. Vital capacity and blood gases do not reliably predict who will need ventilation in MG, so observation in hospital is continuous.

orders.dose: 0.4 g/kg on 5 consecutive days, or 1 g/kg on 2 days
Typically 5 to 10 treatments until stable (German guideline); usually 4 to 6 exchanges (Front Neurol review)
orders.note: The German guideline gives 5 to 10 treatments until stable; the Front Neurol review usually 4 to 6.

orders.dose: Plasma exchange is contraindicated in sepsis; IVIG in hypercoagulability, renal failure or immunoglobulin hypersensitivity
Gilhus 2024 (Nordic): stop during a crisis to limit secretions and plugging, restart before weaning; the Mestinon label says crisis calls for more
orders.note: The 2024 Nordic guidance stops pyridostigmine during a crisis to prevent mucus and airway plugging, restarting it before weaning, and the 2020 review says it may worsen secretions; the Mestinon label, citing 1960s work, says myasthenic crisis suggests the need for more intensive anticholinesterase therapy (StatPearls on neostigmine says the same).

orders.dose: Added alongside IVIG or plasma exchange, not alone; very high doses as add-on in intensive care for a delayed (over 1 week) or insufficient response
Vital capacity and blood gases do not reliably predict the need for respiratory support in MG
Avoid in MG: they can exacerbate the weakness
Use aminoglycosides with caution in MG (they can aggravate weakness); magnesium prolongs paralysis in MG

nodes.summary: Myasthenic crisis: intensive care, IVIG or plasma exchange, and the trigger treated (infection treated without fluoroquinolones or aminoglycosides, culprit drugs stopped). The 2024 Nordic guidance stops pyridostigmine during the crisis and restarts it before weaning; the Mestinon label, citing 1960s work, says the opposite. Afterwards immunotherapy is usually intensified, and thymectomy waits until the patient is off the ventilator and stable.

nodes.ask: Alert and afebrile; cranial nerve palsies, then descending weakness. Next?
options: Call public health now for antitoxin; draw serum before it runs
Plasma exchange to clear the circulating toxin from the blood
IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days to neutralize circulating toxin
Skin-test for horse serum allergy before ordering the equine antitoxin
nodes.chainStep: Call the local or state health department emergency line now for an expert consult and BAT from CDC; serum (no anticoagulant), stool and gastric specimens, serum before BAT; BAT one vial IV in adults as early as possible on clinical grounds; epinephrine at hand; serial neuro and respiratory checks
nodes.why: Suspected botulism is treated with antitoxin on clinical grounds, as early as possible and best within 2 days, because laboratory confirmation takes days and can be negative. The health department arranges the consult and releases antitoxin from CDC. Serum is drawn before the antitoxin, which neutralizes the toxin, but the antitoxin is never delayed for a specimen. Plasmapheresis has shown no clear benefit, immune globulin and plasma exchange are the treatments for GBS, and skin testing is no longer recommended.

orders.dose: Call the local or state health department emergency on-call line at once for an expert consultation and antitoxin from CDC

nodes.summary: Wound botulism: antitoxin as early as possible, the wound debrided and its infection treated as the clinical situation requires (penicillin G or metronidazole for a wound source), and the health department involved. Aminoglycosides can worsen the paralysis.

Foodborne or source-unknown botulism: antitoxin on clinical grounds, the health department called at once so the food and anyone else who ate it can be traced, serum sent before the antitoxin, and serial breathing checks; no exposure history does not rule it out. Paralysis lasts weeks to months, and with intensive care almost all survive.

nodes.why: Infant botulism is treated with human-derived botulism immune globulin (BabyBIG), given as soon as the clinical diagnosis is made and obtained through the California Department of Public Health program; BAT is the antitoxin for other toxin types and for older patients. Antibiotics are not indicated and aminoglycosides worsen the weakness. Stool is collected by enema with sterile water, not with glycerin suppositories. About half need intubation, so the threshold is low.

nodes.why: Functional weakness is inconsistent, with normal reflexes and a positive Hoover sign (the weak leg presses down when the other leg lifts against resistance). The symptoms are real and not intentional. Confronting the patient, or calling it just psychological, is what the source warns against, and medication is for a comorbid anxiety or depression, not a substitute for therapy. Psychotherapy, mainly CBT, is first line, with physiotherapy alongside, and frequent follow-up is one of the most important parts of treatment; there is nothing for IVIG to treat.

cases.label: GBS with failing breathing
